# Pityriasis rosea

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Dermatology > Idiopathic disorders > Pityriasis rosea*

[Original Article Link](/library/Pk0WLT)

---

## Summary

Pityriasis rosea is a common, often pruritic <u>rash</u>. The initial eruption manifests as a single ovoid <u>macule</u> (<u>herald patch</u>) and is followed by a secondary eruption of multiple scaly <u>papules</u> distributed in a classic Christmas tree pattern on the trunk. Patients may experience a <u>flu-like</u> <u>prodrome</u>. Pityriasis rosea is thought to be triggered by a viral infection and most commonly affects young adults, especially female individuals. Diagnosis is clinical. Lesions usually resolve without intervention within 6–12 weeks; <u>management of pruritus</u> may include <u>emollients</u>, <u>topical steroid</u> creams, and/or oral <u>antihistamines</u>. For persistent, severe, or widespread disease, treatment with <u>acyclovir</u> may be considered. Specialist consultation is indicated for pregnant individuals with <u>rash</u> onset before 15 weeks' <u>gestation</u>, who have an increased risk of negative <u>pregnancy</u> outcomes (e.g., <u>preterm birth</u>, <u>stillbirth</u>, <u>spontaneous abortion</u>).

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* A viral etiology (<u>HHV 6</u> and <u>HHV 7</u>) is suspected based on the following: [[2]](/library/88bOov)

* Pityriasis rosea can occur in <u>clusters</u>, affecting many people living in the same community.

* Seasonal variations (more common in the spring and fall)

* Preceded by a <u>prodromal</u> <u>flu-like</u> illness in some patients

* Life-long <u>immunity</u> (recurrence is rare but possible)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Prodrome</u>:  (1–2 weeks prior to <u>rash</u>;  onset): <u>flu-like</u> symptoms (e.g., <u>malaise</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>pharyngitis</u>)

* Initial eruption (∼ 90% of affected individuals): herald patch (<u>mother patch</u>) ;  [[1]](/library/9ubNtv)

* Single ovoid <u>macule</u> or patch, 1–5 cm in diameter

* Slightly raised, dark red border with a central salmon-colored clearing zone  [[4]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[5]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Lesion surrounded by a collarette: a ring-like, fine, white scale (like cigarette paper)  [[6]](/library/X5d9iq0)

* Typically on the trunk

* Secondary eruption (2–21 days later) ;  [[1]](/library/9ubNtv)[[2]](/library/88bOov)

* Bilateral diffuse, oval-shaped <u>papules</u> and <u>plaques</u> (< 1.5 cm) with scaly <u>collarette</u>   

* Salmon-colored in individuals with light <u>skin</u>

* May be <u>hyperpigmented</u> in individuals with dark <u>skin</u>

* <u>Papules</u> appear along <u>Langer lines</u>, which align on the back like the branches of a Christmas tree (Christmas tree appearance)

* <u>Rash</u> typically occurs on the trunk, neck, and upper extremities; scalp and face are more likely to be affected in individuals with dark <u>skin</u> than in individuals with light <u>skin</u>.

* <u>Pruritus</u> occurs in 80–90% of affected individuals. [[3]](/library/5Rdinp0)

* Postinflammatory <u>hypopigmentation</u> or <u>hyperpigmentation</u>, especially for individuals with dark <u>skin</u>





> [!TIP]
> Atypical pityriasis rosea manifests with variation in <u>rash</u> appearance (e.g., <u>vesicular</u>), distribution (e.g., face, scalp, groin, <u>axilla</u>), size of lesions (e.g., small <u>papular</u> lesions, giant lesions), and/or number of lesions. [[2]](/library/88bOov)

## Diagnosis

* Diagnosis is clinical.

* Consider the following for diagnostic uncertainty, atypical manifestation, and/or persistent (> 3 months) <u>rash</u>:

* <u>Diagnostics for dermatophyte infections</u> (e.g., <u>KOH test</u>) to exclude <u>tinea</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for syphilis</u> to exclude <u>secondary syphilis</u>

* <u>Skin biopsy</u>  [[3]](/library/5Rdinp0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Tinea corporis</u>

* <u>Pityriasis versicolor</u>

* Drug eruptions

* <u>Psoriasis</u>

* <u>Lichen planus</u>

* <u>Secondary syphilis</u>

* For details, see “<u>Maculopapular rashes</u>” and “<u>Overview of annular skin lesions</u>.”





![Secondary syphilis](media/lqcdgc3fyqhssa13g2otp4j7.jpg)

Secondary syphilis




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

* Advise patients that spontaneous resolution typically occurs within 6–12 weeks. [[1]](/library/9ubNtv)[[4]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* Consider symptomatic treatment for <u>pruritus</u> as necessary, although evidence to support these treatments, all of which are <u>off-label</u>, is limited. [[3]](/library/5Rdinp0)[[7]](/library/fkdkMJ0)

* Topical <u>emollient</u> (e.g., <u>calamine lotion</u>)

* <u>Topical corticosteroid</u>

* <u>Acyclovir</u>   [[2]](/library/88bOov)[[7]](/library/fkdkMJ0)

* Consider in <u>pityriasis rosea in pregnancy</u> or persistent (> 3 months), severe, or relapsing <u>rash</u>.

* Avoid in children and <u>breastfeeding</u> patients.

* Oral <u>antihistamine</u>

* Oral <u>macrolide</u>, e.g., <u>erythromycin</u>

* <u>UVB phototherapy</u> (severe disease)





> [!TIP]
> Relapse, while rare, typically occurs within 5–18 months. [[1]](/library/9ubNtv)
